772.name: Citizenship - what's it all about?
772.description: In this unit pupils consider what citizenship is all about, they will explore what knowledge and skills they need to develop to become active citizens.
772.why: This unit provides an introduction to some of the key citizenship concepts that pupils will study throughout their citizenship journey. Building on knowledge from the primary curriculum, students consider their existing knowledge on concepts such as democracy, rights and responsibilities and active citizenship and explore how this knowledge will be expanded through studying citizenship.
prior: Pupils know to listen to the opinions of others.
Pupils are familiar with British values, such as democracy and liberty.
Pupils know how Citizenship is different to other subjects.
threads: Active citizenship, making a positive difference

774.name: What are our identities and our communities?
774.description: This unit introduces pupils to the concepts of identities and communities and how these change over time and contexts.
774.why: Pupils learn about their identities and communities because they are beginning to understand the world around them. Understanding identities and community and diverse perspectives is crucial as their sense of belonging develops. This knowledge helps them appreciate how identities and communities change over time and helps to build a strong sense of interconnection and community.
prior: Pupils know that their actions affect themselves and others, to care about other people's feelings and to try to see things from their points of view.
Pupils know to recognise and challenge stereotypes.
Pupils know the differences and similarities between people arise from a number of factors, including cultural, ethnic, racial and religious diversity, gender and disability.
Pupils appreciate the range of national, regional, religious and ethnic identities in the United Kingdom.

803.name: What rights should all children have?
803.description: This unit introduces what rights we are all entitled to and how citizens can protect their rights. Pupils look in more depth at the right to health and the right to accurate information.
803.why: Pupils learn about the rights all children should have because they are developing a sense of justice and equity. Understanding children's rights is crucial for their awareness of global issues. This knowledge helps them recognize the importance of rights, advocate for themselves and others, and foster a fair and compassionate outlook as they develop as informed and responsible citizens.
prior: Pupils know how to recognise what they like and dislike, what is fair and unfair, and what is right and wrong.
Pupils know that there are different kinds of responsibilities, rights and duties at home, at school and in the community, and that these can sometimes conflict with each other.

940.name: How does local democracy work?
940.description: This unit explores the difference between local and national government. Pupils consider how governments are elected, the role of local councils and the key people within them.
940.why: Pupils learn about the differences between local and national government because they are starting to grasp how the political system works and impacts their lives. Understanding these differences is crucial for their civic awareness and participation in democracy. This knowledge helps them recognize the distinct roles and responsibilities of each level of government, fostering informed and active citizenship as they begin to engage with politcal and social ideas affecting communities and broader society.
prior: Pupils know that they belong to various groups and communities, such as family and school.
Pupils know about participation in decision making. E.g. school councils.

941.name: What is crime?
941.description: Pupils consider what crime is, what causes criminal behaviour and how communities can help prevent crime. They also explore whether youth crime is really as serious as the media portrays.
941.why: Pupils learn about what crime is because they are beginning to understand the rules and laws that help govern society. Understanding what constitutes a crime and its impact is crucial for their sense of justice and responsibility. This knowledge helps them recognize the importance of law, the consequences of crime, and the role of the justice system in protecting citizens including young people and maintaining order.

1158.name: How can we make a difference in our communities?
1158.description: In this unit pupils examine what community means and the role it plays at their school. They explore what charities and NGOs do in their community and identify how they can become active citizens.
1158.why: Building on their learning of how they can make a positive difference in their communities this unit continues to develop pupils’ knowledge of social issues and the role citizens and organisations have in creating positive change. This knowledge helps pupils to understand how citizens can work together to improve communities and wider society and how they can make their voice heard by those in positions of power.
prior: Pupils know they belong to various groups and communities, such as family and school.
Pupils recognise the role of voluntary, community and pressure groups.
Pupils know there are different kinds of responsibilities, rights and duties at home, at school and in the community, and that these can sometimes conflict with each other.
threads: Active citizenship, making a positive difference

1828.name: How does the rule of law contribute to fairness?
1828.description: This unit explores how the rule of law operates in society. Pupils examine equality before the law, judicial independence, legal certainty and access to justice, and how these support fairness and trust.
1828.why: This unit develops pupils’ understanding of the rule of law by moving from defining it to examining how it operates through systems and institutions. It builds on KS2 knowledge of fairness and prepares pupils to evaluate how these systems function and can be challenged.
prior: Pupils understand that the rule of law means everyone follows the law.
Pupils know laws help maintain fairness and safety.
Pupils understand that laws apply equally to everyone.
Pupils recognise that people can get help if laws are broken.
Pupils can describe fairness beyond personal situations.

1069.name: How does the political system work in the UK?
1069.description: In this unit, pupils learn about the roles of government and parliament and how they are organised. They explore how elections work and what the role of political parties and MPs are.
1069.why: Pupils learn about how the political system works in the UK as they build their awareness of democracy and government. Understanding the structure and function of the UK political system is crucial for their development as informed citizens. This knowledge helps them grasp how political decisions are made within parliamentary democracy, the checks and balances within different branches of government, and the importance of citizen participation in elections and democracy.
prior: Pupils know about voting and registering to vote.
Pupils know about government, such as local government.
Pupils know the difference between local and national government.

1070.name: How does the media affect us?
1070.description: In this unit students explore the roles and responsibilities of the media and the important role it plays within society.
1070.why: Pupils learn about how the media affects us as they are increasingly exposed to various media and information sources. Understanding media influence, bias, and the importance of truth is crucial for developing critical thinking skills. This knowledge helps them discern reliable information, recognize bias, and understand the media's role in informing and shaping public opinion and holding those in power to account.
prior: Pupils know about different sources of the news.
Pupils know that for most people the internet is an integral part of life and has many benefits.
Pupils know how to be a discerning consumer of information online including understanding that information
threads: Role of media and digital democracy

1071.name: What is the law and how is it changed?
1071.description: In this unit, pupils explore what the law is and how criminal and civil laws are made. They examine what role citizens can have in changing the law and consider how the justice system should apply to young people.
1071.why: Pupils learn about what the law is and how it is changed because they are beginning to understand the structure of society and their role within it. Understanding the legal system and the process of lawmaking is crucial for their development as informed citizens. This knowledge helps them grasp the importance of laws, how they evolve to reflect societal values, and how individuals and groups can influence legal change, preparing them for active participation in their communities.
prior: Pupils know why and how rules and laws are made and enforced.
Pupils know why different rules are needed in different situations and how to take part in making and changing rules.

1073.name: How can citizens bring about change?
1073.description: In this unit, pupils explore the different ways citizens can take action and what role this plays in democracy.
1073.why: Pupils learn about the role of citizens and groups in shaping and improving communities. Pupils build on their foundational knowledge of democracy, rights and equity as they explore different methods of democratic participation and influencing change.
prior: Pupils understand the term democracy.
Pupils understand precious liberties.
Pupils recognise the role of voluntary, community and pressure groups.
threads: Active citizenship, making a positive difference

1074.name: Why was the struggle for the vote important today?
1074.description: Pupils analyse how political rights have changed over time considering important campaigns such as the fight for female suffrage. They examine why voting matters and consider what role they can have in democracy prior to being eligible to vote.
1074.why: Pupils learn about the struggle for the vote because it is essential to understand the foundations of modern democracy, equality and representation. Understanding the historical context highlights the value of democracy and how it develop and changes over time. This knowledge helps them appreciate the significance of voting rights, active citizenship and change, and fosters an awareness of the importance to pursue equity.
prior: Pupils know the meaning of the term democracy.
Pupils know about methods of participation in a democracy, such as voting.
Pupils know about types of elections, such as local elections.

1075.name: What can we do about global problems?
1075.description: Using a range of case studies from human rights to fracking and climate action, pupils consider how they can take responsible action to tackle some of the challenges currently facing society.
1075.why: Pupils learn about global problems and challenges as they develop a broader awareness of the world. Understanding complex issues that interconnect people and the planet such as climate change, poverty and inequality is crucial for fostering a sense of shared responsibility. This knowledge empowers them as they consider the actions that governments and those in power can take. Alongside this they consider our own choices and decisions, and learn how they can be part of positive change, promoting a sense of collaboration, responsibility and global citizenship.
prior: Pupils know about the role of NGOs, pressure groups and charities.
Pupils know about different ways active citizens can bring about change.

1076.name: How is the UK governed?
1076.description: Pupils explore the difference between local, regional and national governance and compare the political systems in the UK and US.
1076.why: Building on their knowledge from Year 7 and 8 about the political system and the law, pupils in Year 9 learn about how the UK is governed as they develop political literacy. Understanding the structure of the UK government, including the roles of Parliament, the Prime Minister, and the judiciary, is crucial for their development as informed citizens. This knowledge helps them grasp how laws are made, how government functions, and the importance of democratic participation, preparing them for active and engaged citizenship.
prior: Pupils know the difference between government and parliament.
Pupils know how elections work.
Pupils know about the role of political parties.

1077.name: Are people treated equally in UK society?
1077.description: Pupils examine what discrimination is and how the law protects people against it, and consider what we can do to create a fairer society and how the UK has progressed in terms of equality.
1077.why: Building on their understanding of rights and communities from Year 7 and 8, pupils in Year 9 learn about whether people are treated equally in UK society as they deepen their awareness of social justice, inclusion and equity. This knowledge helps them recognize discrimination including different racism, appreciate and value diversity, and advocate for a fairer society.
prior: Pupils know about the importance of the law.
Pupils know about the difference between criminal and civil law.

1078.name: Why do people move around the world?
1078.description: Pupils consider why people migrate, the impact it has on communities, whether migration should be controlled and what support is available to migrants.
1078.why: Pupils learn about the different reasons why people move around the world as they develop a global perspective and understanding of migration. Building on earlier lessons about communities and global issues, understanding the complexity of migration is crucial for their awareness of diversity and change in communities and society. This knowledge helps them understand the economic, evironmental, social, and political factors driving migration, the complexities of migration globally as well as its impact on societies and the value of human rights and community cohesion.
prior: Pupils know about human rights.
Pupils know about global challenges, such as climate change.

1079.name: How can we manage money well?
1079.description: Pupils explore how to look after their money considering the implications of borrowing, how they can keep track of their money, what saving options are available to them and what their rights are as a consumer.
1079.why: Pupils are becoming increasingly indepdent and will be considering future financial responsibilities. Learning to manage money now equips them with essential knolwledge and skills in relation to budgeting, saving, and making informed financial decisions in the future. They begin to connect personal financial choices and decisions with the understanding the economy, resources and their role in society as consumers, taxpayers and savers.
prior: Pupils know that money comes from different sources and can be used for different purposes.
Pupils know to look after their money and realise that future wants and needs may be met through saving.

1080.name: Can digital democracy increase political participation?
1080.description: Pupils consider what a digital citizen is and how the digital world can be used to increase political engagement, examining cases of how digital democracy has worked across the globe.
1080.why: Exploring digital democracy now helps pupils understand how digital tools can enhance political participation and engagement. This unit is timely as it prepares pupils to navigate rights related issues, and contribute to the evolving digital political landscape, empowering them to be informed and active citizens. By learning these concepts early, pupils can effectively participate in democratic processes, making this education relevant and impactful.
prior: Pupils know what democracy is, and about the basic institutions that support it locally and nationally.
Pupils know that our lives increasingly involve being online.
threads: Role of media and digital democracy

1082.name: How can young people play an active role in democracy?
1082.description: Pupils consider what role they can play in their communities from school to local and national democracy.
1082.why: Learning how young people can play an active role in democracy equips pupils with the knowledge and skills to engage in civic activities and influence decision-making. This unit is timely as it empowers pupils to understand how they can have a voice, exercise their rights and responsibilities, and the impact they can have on their communities and beyond.
prior: Pupils know about the role of active citizens.
Pupils know about the functions of local democracy.
Pupils know about the importance of participation and listening to the opinions of others.
threads: Active citizenship, making a positive difference

1137.name: How are community identities changing?
1137.description: In this unit pupils explore the concepts of identity, community, migration and belonging.
1137.why: Building on their learning from key stage 3 pupils explore what makes a community and how the nature of communities can change over time. Understanding the complexity of identities and communities is crucial for their awareness of diversity and their sense of belonging. This learning helps pupils to reflect on their own identities, understanding others and contribute positively in their communities.
prior: Pupils have a general understanding of personal and group identity.
Pupils are familiar with key features of a community, such as shared values, interests, and social roles.
Pupils have an awareness of belonging and how different identities coexist.
Pupils have a basic understanding of why people migrate (e.g. jobs, safety, family) and global connections.

1138.name: What tools can we use to challenge injustice in our communities?
1138.description: Pupils consider a diverse range of case studies to develop their understanding of how and why people challenge injustice in their communities.
1138.why: This unit builds on pupils growing awareness of social issues and their potential roles as active citizens in addressing them. Understanding the tools to challenge injustice in our communities builds on their existing knowledge of civic responsibility and rights. This unit equips pupils with practical strategies and skills for active citizenship.
prior: Pupils know that citizens can take action to bring about change in society.
Pupils know what a community is and how people and organisations work to support it.
Pupils know they have rights and responsibilities as part of a democratic society.
Pupils know that they can play a role in creating a fairer and more inclusive community.

1147.name: What are the strengths and weaknesses of the UK democratic system?
1147.description: Pupils develop their knowledge of democracy and the different types of democracy considering the strengths and weaknesses of the UK system.
1147.why: Pupils learn about the strengths and weaknesses of the UK democratic system and build on their previous knowledge of basic political concepts and structures. This unit deepens their understanding of democracy, encouraging critical thinking about different types of governance and how democracy can be strengthened.
prior: Pupils know the difference between local, regional, and national government.
Pupils know how local councils work and who represents people in their area.
Pupils know there is a difference between government and Parliament.
Pupils know that we elect people to represent us.

1148.name: What are the strengths and weaknesses of the legal system?
1148.description: Pupils learn how laws are made and enforced and about the purpose and types of punishment.
1148.why: This unit builds on pupils foundational understanding of law and its role in society. Pupils examine the strengths and weaknesses of the legal system critically evaluating how laws are applied and enforced in the UK. This knowledge helps them recognise the distinct roles and responsibilities within the legal system, fostering informed and active citizenship as they deepen their level of engagment with politcal and social ideas affecting society.
prior: Pupils can explain what crime is and some causes of criminal behaviour.
Pupils can explain what laws are.
Pupils have a basic understanding of how laws are made.
Pupils have explored the purpose of the justice system.

1149.name: How does the economy work?
1149.description: Pupils learn what the economy is, what taxes are and consider local and central government spending and risk management.
1149.why: This unit builds on prior learning around personal finance and managing money through looking at basic economic concepts and principles. Pupils examines how the UK Government manages its finances and the impact on citizens and public services. By the end, pupils will understand the balance between economic decisions, taxation, and public service provision in the UK.
prior: Pupils can manage basic money skills like budgeting and saving.
Pupils understand the importance of managing money for future independence.
Pupils recognise that government financial decisions affect communities and services.

1141.name: What has the UK economy got to do with me?
1141.description: This unit develops pupils' knowledge and understanding of the UK economy and helps them appreciate its relevance to them.
1141.why: Understanding what the UK economy has to do with them builds on pupils existing knowledge of personal finance and basic economic concepts. The unit helps pupils connect macroeconomic concepts to their personal experiences, such as income, credit, debt and taxation. By learning these concepts now, pupils can better understand how economic policies and trends affect their future decisions and prospects.
prior: Pupils understand basic personal finance concepts like income, saving, and spending
Pupils know about credit, debt, and how they affect personal finances.
Pupils recognise the role of taxes and why people pay them.
Pupils can connect economic policies to their own lives and future decisions.

1145.name: How does the media hold those in power to account?
1145.description: Pupils consider what role the media plays in democracy and how the media is used to hold those in power to account. They consider what responsible journalism is and the impact of misinformation.
1145.why: Building on their key stage three learning about how the media impacts them this unit explores the important role the media plays within democracy. Through exploring concepts such as responsible journalism, censorship and misinformation pupils critically consider the importance of a free press to society.
prior: Pupils can explain why it is important to check if information is true and reliable.
Pupils know that the media plays a role in shaping society and public opinion.
Pupils recognise that media can have bias and affect how information is presented.
threads: Role of media and digital democracy

1146.name: How can we make a difference in society? Active citizenship project
1146.description: Pupils are introduced to what an active citizenship project is, how it should be structured and the skills they need to complete one.
1146.why: Building on their learning of how they can make a positive difference in their communities this unit continues to develop pupils’ knowledge of social issues and the role citizens and organisations have in creating positive change. This knowledge helps pupils to understand how citizens can work together to improve communities and wider society and how they can make their voice heard by those in positions of power.
prior: Pupils understand there are different ways citizens can make a positive difference in their communities
Pupils can explain how young people can take part in democracy and influence decisions.
Pupils can identify opportunities to get involved and work with others to create change.
threads: Active citizenship, making a positive difference

1829.name: Why is the rule of law important?
1829.description: This unit analyses how the rule of law operates in contemporary Britain. Pupils evaluate threats to fairness, including inequality, abuse of power and barriers to justice, and examine the role of citizens in upholding the law.
1829.why: This unit builds on pupils’ understanding of legal systems by focusing on evaluation and application in real-world contexts.
prior: Pupils understand the key principles of the rule of law.
Pupils know laws should be applied equally and fairly.
Pupils understand the role of courts and judges.
Pupils recognise that people can challenge unfairness.
Pupils can analyse examples of fairness and inequality in society.

1139.name: Should the UK be called a democracy?
1139.description: Pupils consider what makes a democracy, they explore key features of democracy in the UK and consider how those in power are held to account.
1139.why: This unit builds on pupils prior learning about what a democracy is. Pupils take a more in-depth look at how democracy works in the UK by exploring what parliament is, how we can hold those in power to account and the role of the press and media and select committees within democracy. The unit encourages critical thinking about governance, representation and citizens rights.
prior: Pupils should understand what democracy means and the key features that define it.
Pupils should recognise the structure and role of the UK Parliament.
Pupils should have a general awareness of the media’s role in society and the importance of free press.
Pupils should be familiar with the concept of devolution and its impact on governance.
Pupils should understand basic democratic participation methods and how citizens can get involved.

1135.name: How can politicians involve citizens in direct decision making?
1135.description: Through a series of case studies from across the globe pupils explore different methods of direct democracy and consider how UK citizens can play a part in shaping national policy.
1135.why: Understanding how politicians can involve citizens in direct decision-making builds on pupils knowledge of politics, parliament and government and their active citizenship skills. This unit is timely as it highlights mechanisms like referendums and consultations, exploring different methods for citizens to make their voices heard. By learning these concepts now, pupils can advocate for and participate in direct democratic processes now and in the future.
prior: Pupils know how the UK political system, parliament, and government work.
Pupils have explored the role of citizens in democracy and how they can participate.
Pupils understand different ways citizens can influence decisions and the importance of active engagement.

1126.name: How can we play a part in the legal system?
1126.description: Pupils consider a range of roles within the legal system, explore what rights citizens have within the justice system and what influence they can have on the law.
1126.why: Learning how they can play a part in the legal system builds on pupils' knowledge of law and governance. This unit is timely as it highlights opportunities for active participation, such as jury duty, volunteering, or legal advocacy. This knowledge helps pupils understand the role of citizens in the justice system, preparing them for active and engaged citizenship.
prior: Pupils understand basic legal rights and the structure of the justice system.
Pupils know how laws are made and the importance of citizen involvement.
Pupils have have explored key roles in law and government.

1127.name: What can we do to reduce crime?
1127.description: Pupils explore how crime impacts the UK and consider the purpose of sentencing and whether current sentencing approaches in the UK are effective.
1127.why: Understanding what can be done to reduce crime builds on their knowledge of rights, justice and the law. This unit explores strategies for crime prevention and rehabilitation. By learning these concepts now, pupils can contribute to creating safer communities through informed actions and advocacy.
prior: Pupils know why laws exist.
Pupils understand the role of the justice system.
Pupils have have explored rights and responsibilities related to the justice system.

1131.name: How powerful is the media?
1131.description: Pupils explore the power and influence of the media both locally and nationally and consider how citizens can effectively navigate the information they are presented with.
1131.why: Understanding how powerful the media is builds on pupils knowledge of the media and its role within a democractic society. This unit is timely as it examines the media's role in shaping perceptions, influencing policy, and holding power to account. By learning these concepts now, pupils can critically evaluate media content and its impact on society, preparing them to be media literate and informed citizens.
prior: Pupils understand the media’s role and responsibilities in society.
Pupils know how media can influence opinions and the importance of truth.
Pupils have considered how media shapes views locally and nationally.
threads: Role of media and digital democracy

1132.name: How is social media changing our view of democracy?
1132.description: Pupils consider the impact that new forms of media are having on democracy using case studies from the UK and India.
1132.why: Understanding how social media is changing our view of democracy builds on pupils' knowledge of governance and media influence. This unit is timely as it explores the impact of social media on political engagement, information dissemination, and public opinion. By learning these concepts now, pupils can critically assess digital media's role in democracy, making this education crucial for developing informed and discerning citizens.
prior: Pupils know the media’s role in democracy and how it shapes public opinion.
Pupils understand digital media as a source of information and influence.
Pupils have explored different means of political engagement.
threads: Role of media and digital democracy

1125.name: How do democratic systems work around the world?
1125.description: Pupils explore how key democratic structures such as the justice system, the media and government operate across the globe and consider the impact this has on human rights and citizens ability to take action.
1125.why: Learning how democratic systems work around the world builds on their knowledge of government and democracy within the UK. This unit provides a comparative perspective on different democratic practices and institutions. By exploring these concepts now, pupils can appreciate the diversity of democratic systems and critically consider the pros and cons of different democractic systems.
prior: Pupils understand how democracy works in the UK, including government, law, and media roles.
Pupils know what human rights are and how they are protected in law.
Pupils have learned about local and national governance and the importance of active participation.

1150.name: How does the UK play a role in the international community?
1150.description: Pupils consider the role the UK plays in Europe and the wider world, exploring organisations such as the United Nations and WTO and examining what role the UK has in global problems.
1150.why: Understanding how the UK plays a role in the international community builds on pupils' knowledge of politics and global issues. This unit is timely as it explores the UK's contributions to international organizations, diplomacy, and global challenges. By learning these concepts now, pupils can better understand the UK's global impact and their role as global citizens.
prior: Pupils understand the UK’s political system and governance.
Pupils have considered global issues.
Pupils can see their role as active global citizens who can engage with international issues.

1140.name: How can I be a changemaker in my community?
1140.description: This unit enables students to build knowledge and understanding of communities and develop active citizenship skills to make a positive change.
1140.why: Learning how to be a changemaker in their local community builds on pupils' knowledge of active citizenship. This unit provides practical tools and strategies for community engagement and advocacy. By exploring these concepts now, pupils are empowered to take initiative and drive positive change in their communities, preparing them to be active and engaged citizens.
prior: Pupils have explored the meaning of active citizenship and ways to make a difference in their communities.
Pupils understand identities, rights, and responsibilities in society.
Pupils have explored community issues and explored local issues and the ways people can participate to make a positive difference.
threads: Active citizenship, making a positive difference

1152.name: What is the nature of the British Constitution?
1152.description: In this unit pupils consider why we need a separation of powers and whether the current political structures are fit for purpose.
1152.why: Building on earlier units on democracy and the UK political system, this unit further explores the nature of the British constitution. The unit provides critical insights into how the UK political system operates encouraging students to think critically about the pros and cons of the current system. Understanding the nature of the British constitution is essential learning for informed civic participation.
prior: Pupils understand the key features of the UK democratic system and how it operates.
Pupils explain the roles of government, Parliament, and local authorities.
Pupils can evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the UK democratic system.

1156.name: Where does power reside in the UK?
1156.description: Pupils look at the role of local and national government and identify reserved and devolved powers in the UK.
1156.why: Pupils explore the distribution of power within their country. Understanding where power resides in the UK builds on their knowledge of power and government. By exploring these concepts now, pupils can critically evaluate how power is allocated and exercised and how they can bring their voice to power, preparing them for informed participation in civic life.
prior: Pupils should understand the basic difference between local and national government.
Pupils should know that some powers are transferred to Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland.
Pupils should recognise the roles and structures of different levels of government.
Pupils should have a basic understanding of UK elections and voting processes.

1155.name: How do others govern?
1155.description: Pupils compare different types of government from the UK to US and North Korea.
1155.why: Understanding how others govern builds on pupils' existing knowledge of the UK political system. This unit broadens pupils comparative understanding of different governmental structures and practices worldwide. By exploring these concepts now, pupils can critically assess the effectiveness of various governance models and examine the diversity of political systems and the impact this has.
prior: Pupils should understand key features of democratic government and how it operates in the UK.
Pupils should be familiar with the structure and roles of UK Parliament and government.
Pupils should know how elections work in the UK and their importance.
Pupils should have a basic grasp of political leadership roles, such as the Prime Minister.

1481.name: How do we look after an ageing population?
1481.description: Pupils explore what role financial systems play in our communities, they consider what personal responsibility they have for financial planning and what role government plays in this, focussing on the impact our ageing population has on financial planning.
1481.why: In this unit pupils take their existing knowledge on personal and public finances and consider how our financial systems are responding to the changing population and the impact this is having. The unit builds on knowledge of both personal and government spending and encourages students to think critically about spending responsibilities across society.
prior: Types of saving and investments
Different types of taxes collected by the government
How government spends taxes
How the UK government prevents and manages risk

1488.name: How can we prepare well for financial decision making?
1488.description: Using the example of housing, pupils explore a range of different financial decisions, products and services. They consider how they can prepare to become financially independent and what advice is available to them.
1488.why: This unit builds on pupils existing knowledge of personal and public spending and their understanding of debt, credit loans, savings investment and risk. Using the example of housing, students critically consider how personal and public spending and economic decisions can impact housing nationally.
prior: What credit and loans are
What local authorities and national government fund
Financial challenges local and national government have
What taxes are and why we pay them
How citizens can support a healthy economy
What debt is

1143.name: What are the different ways we can become involved in politics?
1143.description: Pupils build knowledge and understanding of political systems, government, voting and elections. Pupils consider the vast range of political roles, exploring the impact that these roles can have across local communities and wider society and how they can get involved in politics.
1143.why: Building on their growing knowledge of democracy, this unit further develops students understanding of political systems and civic engagement. The unit provides insight into how the UK political system and political systems around the world operate and examines the skills needed for a variety of roles within politics. This knowledge helps them to recognise the distinct roles and responsibilities within politics, fostering informed and active citizenship.
prior: Pupils understand the key features of a democratic system and the role of elected representatives in the UK.
Pupils know how elections work and how citizens can participate in democratic processes.
Pupils have examined how the media holds those in power to account and the importance of a free press.
Pupils have started to consider their own role in society and how they can take part in political and community action.

1151.name: How is UK society diverse and changing?
1151.description: Pupils explore what identity is and how the UK population is changing considering how diverse the UK is and exploring mutual respect and understanding between different groups within society.
1151.why: Building on prior learning around identities and communities this unit analyses what identity is, how it can evolve over time and the impact this has on the population and communities in the UK. Through exploring these concepts now pupils can better understand and engage with a range of diverse communities, preparing them to be informed and active citizens.
prior: Pupils know what identity means and how individual and group identities are shaped.
Pupils have examined the role of communities in shaping identity and the importance of mutual respect, inclusion, and shared values.
Pupils have considered how social change and migration contribute to the diversity of UK society and how communities respond to change.
Pupils have developed an understanding of the challenges and opportunities that come with living in a diverse society.

1153.name: Why do we need the right to protest in a democracy?
1153.description: Pupils explore how rights have developed in the UK and how they are protected. They look at what changes in society have occurred due to protest.
1153.why: Understanding the necessity of the right to protest in a democracy builds on pupils' knowledge of rights, justice and the law and their knowledge of active citizenship. This unit explores the role of protest in influencing change and protecting freedoms. It challenges pupils to critically consider what methods are acceptable to create change, supporting them to develop as informed and responsible citizens.
prior: Pupils understand the concept of legal rights and how they are protected through UK law.
Pupils know how citizens can participate in democracy, including through direct action and campaigning.
Pupils can identify how individuals and groups influence change within democratic systems.

1129.name: How does identity affect rights?
1129.description: This unit introduces pupils to the concept of multiply identities, pupils consider what impact different identities can have on rights.
1129.why: Understanding how identity affects rights builds on pupils' awareness of diversity and equality. This unit is timely as it asks pupils to critically think about the intersection of various identities with legal rights. By learning these concepts now, pupils can better advocate for themselves and others.
prior: Pupils have explored what personal and national identity means.
Pupils have They have examined rights and responsibilities, including how the law protects against discrimination.
Pupils have considered migration, diversity, and equality, and how people are treated in UK society.

1142.name: Does our legal system protect citizens' rights?
1142.description: This unit builds pupils knowledge and understanding of the law and the legal system including: criminal and civil justice; the judicial process and role of citizens in justice; legal rights, sanctions; and how well prison works.
1142.why: Understanding how the legal system protects citizens' rights builds on their knowledge of the key concepts of law and rights. This unit takes these concepts and looks at how they relate to each other. By learning to consider these concepts synoptically now, pupils can better understand their rights and the legal protections available to them.
prior: Pupils know why laws exist and the role of the justice system.
Pupils know there are different types of law i.e. criminal and civil.
Pupil have explored the roles of different legal professionals within the justice system.
Pupils understand what rights are and how they are protected in law.

1130.name: How can the local economy support sustainability?
1130.description: Using the example of sustainability, students consider the local economy and its impact on citizens and their local communities.
1130.why: Exploring how the local economy can support sustainability builds on pupils' knowledge of finance and the economy. This unit is timely as it highlights sustainable practices and their importance for future generations. By learning these concepts now, pupils can advocate for and engage in sustainable economic activities.
prior: Pupils understand the role of taxation and government in supporting communities and public services.
Pupils know how citizens can contribute to and shape their local communities through active citizenship.
Pupils can explain the importance of economic decisions in addressing wider issues like sustainability and community wellbeing.

1136.name: How does the international community respond to global humanitarian problems?
1136.description: Pupils consider what role the UK should have in tackling international conflict and global humanitarian problems, exploring different methods for conflict resolution.
1136.why: Understanding the international community's response to global humanitarian problems builds on pupils' knowledge of UK and the wider world. This unit is timely as it examines mechanisms and strategies for addressing crises. By learning these concepts now, pupils can appreciate the role of international cooperation in solving global challenges, fostering a sense of global citizenship.
prior: Pupils understand how the UK engages with international organisations such as the UN, NATO and the Commonwealth.
Pupils can explain how citizens and governments contribute to solving societal problems, including through active citizenship and advocacy.
Pupils know how global issues can be addressed through cooperation and the role the UK plays in international responses.

1128.name: How well has the UK adjusted to its changing relationship with the EU?
1128.description: Pupils analyse the reasons behind the Brexit referendum and consider what the implications of it have been.
1128.why: Understanding how the UK has adjusted to its changing relationship with the EU builds on pupils' knowledge of the UK and the wider world. This unit is timely as it explores the political, economic, and social adjustments post-Brexit. By learning these concepts now, pupils can critically evaluate the impacts and ongoing challenges
prior: Pupils know the role of citizens in democracy and understand how they can participate through mechanisms like referendums.
Pupils understand the UK's role in international organisations and their potential influence on global issues.

1133.name: How effective is the UN and SDGs on promoting sustainability?
1133.description: Pupils consider what role international organisations play in sustainability and climate justice.
1133.why: Understanding the effectiveness of the UN on climate change builds on pupils' knowledge of the UK and the wider world. This unit assesses international efforts to combat climate change. By learning these concepts now, pupils can critically evaluate the UN's role and efficacy. This supports pupils to develop informed and researched opinions toward sustainability.
prior: Pupils know how the UK engages with global organisations and its role in international cooperation.
Pupils understand the impact of political decision-making on global and national issues.
Pupils can explain how citizens and governments influence change at local, national, and international levels.

1123.name: Synopticity: How do different ideas and concepts in Citizenship interconnect?
1123.description: Pupils revisit key citizenship concepts from previous units and consider how they relate to each other, demonstrating their ability to draw together different areas of knowledge, skills and understanding.
1123.why: This unit brings together learning from across the entire sequence. It prepares students for answering extended response questions in their GCSE which will relate to two of more specification themes.
prior: Pupils have studied a broad range of citizenship topics including active citizenship, human rights, politics/parliament/government, law, media, economy, and international relations.
Pupils are prepared to integrate knowledge and skills from across the curriculum to deepen their understanding of citizenship.

1157.name: Practising what we have learnt
1157.description: Pupils revisit a number of the key concepts covered in earlier units in preparation for their GCSE papers.
1157.why: This unit brings together learning from across the entire sequence. It prepares students for answering questions in their GCSE by revisiting the key learning from each thread.
prior: Pupils have covered key concepts from across the GCSE Citizenship course, including rights, democracy, power, identity, justice, and the UK’s global role.
Pupils have developed knowledge and understanding of how these concepts interconnect.

4747.outcome: I can explain how the UK's identity changed over time and how national identities affect the UK today.
points: Immigration and key historical events have significantly influenced the development of UK identity.
Census data reveals a change towards greater religious and ethnic diversity, reflecting a more multicultural society.
Political events such as Brexit have altered how individuals perceive their national identity.
Devolution has enabled nations to govern independently on certain issues, reinforcing distinct national identities.
These evolving identities affect public policy, political engagement and debates over the future structure of the UK.
keywords: descent into a lower or worse state
when a group has people with different backgrounds and experiences; this can be differences in nationality, ethnicity, culture, religion, language, identity, interests, skills and perspectives
who a person is, or the qualities of a person or group that make them different than others

4748.name: How does the justice system work in the UK?
4748.outcome: I can explain what justice means and how justice is carried out in the UK.
points: The UK justice system is based on the rule of law, which ensures fairness and equality for all.
Justice includes access to legal advice, fair trials and support for both the victims and the accused.
Sentences like prison, community orders and fines are used depending on the severity of the crime.
These sentences aim to protect the public, rehabilitate offenders and deter future crime.
Legal professionals help make sure the correct processes are followed and that everyone’s rights are respected.
keywords: fair treatment and equality under the law
the principle that all individuals within a state, including government and leaders, are subject to the same laws and must follow them
the punishment that a judge or magistrate decides someone should be given after they have been convicted of a crime

4749.name: What is the UK's relationship with international organisations?
4749.outcome: I can explain what the main functions, benefits and obligations are of international organisations and their relationship to the UK.
points: The UK is part of key international organisations such as the UN, NATO, WTO, the Commonwealth.
International organisations help with peace, defence, trade and development, both nationally and globally.
Membership gives the UK benefits like influence, trade access, defence support and military training.
The UK also has obligations, like paying membership fees, following rules and upholding shared values.
Working with others through collaboration helps the UK stay safe and respected in the global community.
keywords: a positive result or advantage that the UK gains from being a member of something
a group of countries that agree to work together on shared goals such as peace, trade, defence or development
an act or course of action to which a person is morally or legally bound; a duty or commitment

4750.name: How does the UK Constitution affect the way the country is governed?
4750.outcome: I can explain how the UK Constitution works and how it differs from the Constitution of the United States.
points: The UK has an uncodified constitution, made up of laws, conventions and traditions.
Parliamentary Sovereignty means Parliament can make or change any law.
The UK system is flexible and can respond quickly, like with the Online Safety Act 2023.
The US has a codified constitution, which is written in one document and harder to change.
The US is a federal system, so states control areas like education, unlike the UK's devolved system.
keywords: a constitution is a set of basic principles or laws that govern a nation
accepted rules or practices in a particular type of writing or genre
the laws, legal decisions and customs that govern a country that does not have a constitution in a single written document

1680.belief: Citizenship is only about legal status.
1680.statement: Citizenship is only about legal status.
1680.correction: Citizenship is all about being part of a society and being an active citizen.

4063.belief: Only leaders, or those in power, can be active citizens.
4063.statement: Only leaders, or those in power, can be active citizens.
4063.correction: Whilst leadership skills might help in some situations, many active citizens work behind the scenes, you don’t need to be a leader or in power to be an active citizen.

9034.belief: Rules are the same for everyone.
9034.statement: Rules are the same for everyone.
9034.correction: Rules may be different in different settings and situations, for example, you may have different rules at school and home. Laws are the same for everyone.

2914.belief: Fairness always means treating everybody the same.
2914.statement: Fairness always means treating everybody the same.
2914.correction: Fairness may involve treating people differently based on their individual circumstances in order to achieve equitable outcomes.

2235.belief: Democracy is just about voting for leaders and making decisions by majority rule.
2235.statement: Democracy is just about voting for leaders and making decisions by majority rule.
2235.correction: Democracy is about fairness, equality and everyone having a voice in how their society is run.

4369.belief: To make a difference within the school community an active citizen has to make a big change.
4369.statement: To make a difference within the school community an active citizen has to make a big change.
4369.correction: Even small actions at school can make a meaningful change.

5388.statement: Some people believe that you can only have one identity.
5388.correction: People can have multiple identities because they can belong to different groups at the same time.

3866.belief: Ireland is part of the United Kingdom.
3866.statement: Ireland is part of the United Kingdom.
3866.correction: Ireland is a separate country that gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1922, but Northern Ireland is part of the UK.

1829.correction: Communities are different depending on where they are located and the people they contain. However, in some places, communities have not seen much migration and are not diverse as a result.

1828.belief: Communities do not change and stay the same, regardless of the people in them.
1828.statement: Communities do not change and stay the same, regardless of the people in them.
1828.correction: Communities will always change due to many reasons including migration, politics, demography and the economy.

11188.belief: No young people are represented in Parliament.
11188.statement: No young people are represented in Parliament.
11188.correction: The UK Youth Parliament has been running for 25 years and holds elections to join. These elections are open to all young people aged 11-18. They liaise with Parliament on various issues and campaign for change as a way to be represented nationally.

3321.correction: Globalisation benefits everyone because with collaboration we can achieve more things together as a global community.

8963.belief: We only have rights when we are adults.
8963.statement: We only have rights when we are adults.
8963.correction: We have rights as children as well as adults. Some of these are different but they are all designed to allow everyone to live a safe and happy life.

2803.correction: Some children do not have access to their right to education.

5752.belief: We are powerless to protect the rights of others until we are adults.
5752.statement: We are powerless to protect the rights of others until we are adults.
5752.correction: Children can protect the rights of others by using active citizenship methods.

4877.belief: You need to pay to see a doctor in the UK.
4877.statement: You need to pay to see a doctor in the UK.
4877.correction: The NHS is free in the UK; therefore you can see a doctor for no charge - this protects our right to healthcare. Some people choose to have private healthcare in the UK, but this is a personal choice.

2563.belief: We can easily tell when information is unreliable and inaccurate.
2563.statement: We can easily tell when information is unreliable and inaccurate.
2563.correction: There are several ways that misinformation can convince us that untruths are real without us always realising.

4992.belief: There is nothing that protects and supports children’s rights in the UK.
4992.statement: There is nothing that protects and supports children’s rights in the UK.
4992.correction: There are lots of organisations that protect and support children’s rights in the UK.

4244.correction: Laws are made by central government, which must be followed by local councils. However, they can lobby the central government and influence policy through campaigns, consultations and public pressure.

2058.belief: Councils only deal with minor issues, like park maintenance.
2058.statement: Councils only deal with minor issues, like park maintenance.
2058.correction: Local councils play a crucial role in many significant areas, including urban and housing planning, public health, education and community services. They have a say in local regulations, budgets and initiatives that greatly impact quality of life.

4237.belief: Local councillors are the same as MPs.
4237.statement: Local councillors are the same as MPs.
4237.correction: MPs represent local areas on a national level. Councillors represent residents at a local level within cities, towns or counties. Councillors do not get a say in making laws, like MPs do. Councillors get an allowance, while MPs are paid a salary.

822.belief: All candidates have the same level of resources and support during campaigns.
822.statement: All candidates have the same level of resources and support during campaigns.
822.correction: In reality, some candidates may struggle to reach voters due to limited funding or organisation, which can affect their visibility and chances of success.

2791.belief: Everyone automatically gets a chance to vote in a UK election.
2791.statement: Everyone automatically gets a chance to vote in a UK election.
2791.correction: Not all residents are eligible to vote or are registered to vote. Some may miss out on elections if they don’t register in time or are unaware of the process.

11185.belief: Young people can't have a real influence on local decision making because they are not old enough to vote or be a councillor.
11185.statement: Young people can't have a real influence on local decision making because they are not old enough to vote or be a councillor.
11185.correction: Young people can have a significant impact by speaking up, raising awareness, organising community actions and engaging with local leaders. They can be powerful voices for change, especially when working together and being persistent.

2115.belief: Crimes can only be committed by adults.
2115.statement: Crimes can only be committed by adults.
2115.correction: Anyone can commit a crime. In England, once you reach the age of ten, you can be held criminally responsible for your actions. This means that if a person aged ten or older breaks the law, they can face legal consequences.

529.correction: Criminal behaviour can be influenced by various factors like their environment, the people around them, or their mental state.

5682.belief: The police make up the whole of the justice system.
5682.statement: The police make up the whole of the justice system.
5682.correction: The police are part of the justice system. There are three layers to the justice system: laws, courts and the police.

11186.belief: Most young people are involved in crime because the media shows so many negative stories about them.
11186.statement: Most young people are involved in crime because the media shows so many negative stories about them.
11186.correction: While the media often focuses on negative stories, the majority of young people are not involved in crime. Recent statistics show that many stop and searches and arrests don’t lead to charges, and the number of young people in custody is low.

5683.belief: Only the police can prevent crime.
5683.statement: Only the police can prevent crime.
5683.correction: Communities can also play a key role by using strategies like education, situational changes and deterrents to reduce crime and promote safety.

2114.belief: Crime prevention strategies only work if they catch criminals.
2114.statement: Crime prevention strategies only work if they catch criminals.
2114.correction: Crime prevention strategies are about stopping crime before it happens. For example, strategies like educating young people, improving public spaces and changing attitudes can help reduce the chances of crime occurring in the first place.

1831.belief: Community cohesion comes easily to all communities.
1831.statement: Community cohesion comes easily to all communities.
1831.correction: Community cohesion takes work and effort to maintain relationships and keep everyone together working towards the same goal.

9122.belief: Schools have very little to do with the local community.
9122.statement: Schools have very little to do with the local community.
9122.correction: Schools are often at the centre of local communities, offering opportunities, facilities and events to people in the community as well as educating the young people who live in the community.

1832.belief: Community groups, charities and NGOs do not make much of a difference in local communities.
1832.statement: Community groups, charities and NGOs do not make much of a difference in local communities.
1832.correction: Charities, groups and NGOs make a huge difference and have a measurable impact on local communities and their success.

11182.belief: Young people cannot change anything in their communities, only adults can.
11182.statement: Young people cannot change anything in their communities, only adults can.
11182.correction: Young people, as well as adults, can make lasting change in their communities. Young people have many powerful tools, like social media, to campaign for change.

82.belief: Active citizenship campaigns are not part of democracy.
82.statement: Active citizenship campaigns are not part of democracy.
82.correction: If you work together effectively, active citizen campaign tasks are an important form of taking part in democracy.

4850.belief: It is not necessary for campaigners to have any financial skills.
4850.statement: It is not necessary for campaigners to have any financial skills.
4850.correction: Financial skills are really important in active citizenship campaigns. There are often budgets to stick to, risks to manage and financial reporting to complete.

4048.belief: The law only matters for some people, or only for those who break it.
4048.statement: The law only matters for some people, or only for those who break it.
4048.correction: Use real-life examples, such as school rules vs. national laws, or news stories in which leaders were held accountable, to show the law in action.

3927.belief: Judges or courts just “make it up” or are biased.
3927.statement: Judges or courts just “make it up” or are biased.
3927.correction: Independent courts follow the law and make decisions without outside influence to ensure fairness.

3357.belief: The Government is the same thing as Parliament.
3357.statement: The Government is the same thing as Parliament.
3357.correction: Parliament makes laws and is made up of elected MPs, appointed Lords and the monarch. The Government implements laws and runs the country, led by the PM. Parliament scrutinises Government decisions.

5810.belief: The Prime Minister is directly elected by the public during the general election.
5810.statement: The Prime Minister is directly elected by the public during the general election.
5810.correction: The Prime Minister is not elected by the people; instead, they are the leader of the party that has the most seats in the House of Commons after the election.

5350.belief: The party that wins the most seats will form the Government and have all the power.
5350.statement: The party that wins the most seats will form the Government and have all the power.
5350.correction: If a party does not have the majority of seats (50%+1) in Parliament, they may not be able to form a government. They might have to form a formal coalition or a voting agreement with a smaller party to get the majority. Power may have to be shared.

5685.belief: Political parties are all either left wing or right wing.
5685.statement: Political parties are all either left wing or right wing.
5685.correction: Many parties mix both views or focus on specific issues, like regional concerns. Some parties are centrist or have ideas that don’t fit neatly into either side.

4744.correction: MPs spend a lot of time helping constituents, attending local events and managing casework.

1689.belief: Civil servants and public sector workers make political decisions.
1689.statement: Civil servants and public sector workers make political decisions.
1689.correction: Civil servants and other public sector workers are neutral professionals who work to implement government policies and decisions made by elected ministers, but they do not make political decisions themselves.

2329.belief: Devolved governments can make laws on any issue.
2329.statement: Devolved governments can make laws on any issue.
2329.correction: The powers of devolved governments are limited to specific policy areas defined by devolution agreements.

3292.belief: We all get our news and information from the same place.
3292.statement: We all get our news and information from the same place.
3292.correction: People get their news and information from a range of different media sources which can result in people believing very different stories.

4529.belief: The media can report whatever they like, there are no consequences.
4529.statement: The media can report whatever they like, there are no consequences.
4529.correction: There are consequences for the media breaking the rules and not fulfilling their responsibilities. They have to abide by a strict code of conduct and ethics.

4523.belief: The media doesn’t play a role in democracy and simply reports what the Government tells it.
4523.statement: The media doesn’t play a role in democracy and simply reports what the Government tells it.
4523.correction: The media has an important role in democracy. It sets the agenda by choosing which issues to focus on, helping inform and educate the public. This means the media, not the Government, decides which stories are highlighted and discussed.

2843.belief: There are no examples of the media holding those in power to account.
2843.statement: There are no examples of the media holding those in power to account.
2843.correction: There are many examples of the media holding those in power to account, for example, if a politician makes promises about education and doesn't deliver, the media could publish an article about it to hold them to account.

850.belief: We can't trust anything we see in the media.
850.statement: We can't trust anything we see in the media.
850.correction: We can make sure we know how to get access to reliable and accurate information which will be more trustworthy.

4524.belief: The media always helps the public learn information.
4524.statement: The media always helps the public learn information.
4524.correction: Sometimes we are given misinformation, disinformation or malinformation. It is important to learn to spot this and realise that some of the media we are presented with is not always designed to help the public learn the true facts.

8992.belief: It is the role of the police to make laws.
8992.statement: It is the role of the police to make laws.
8992.correction: Laws are created by Parliament. The police do not make the law, they enforce it.

2117.belief: Criminal law is only for very serious crimes, like murder or robbery.
2117.statement: Criminal law is only for very serious crimes, like murder or robbery.
2117.correction: Whilst criminal law deals with serious crimes like murder and robbery, it also covers a wide range of other offenses, such as theft and vandalism. Criminal law is used when someone's actions harm society, no matter how big or small the crime is.

1679.belief: Citizens have no power to influence the law in the UK.
1679.statement: Citizens have no power to influence the law in the UK.
1679.correction: Citizens in the UK do have the power to influence the law. They can use methods like online petitions, surveys, lobbying politicians and working with the media or charities to bring attention to issues and encourage lawmakers to make changes.

11191.belief: If a young person is accused of a crime, they are treated the same as an adult in court.
11191.statement: If a young person is accused of a crime, they are treated the same as an adult in court.
11191.correction: Young people have some special protections in the legal system, e.g., in youth courts, the focus is on rehabilitation and making sure young people are given the support they need to avoid reoffending. They also have extra rights when arrested.

982.statement: Children under the age of 10 have no consequences for their actions.
982.correction: Whilst the age of criminal responsbility in England, Wales and Northern Ireland is 10, this does not mean children under this age will face no conseqences if they break the law. They may still face other forms of intervention.

187.belief: The age of criminal responsibility is the same worldwide.
187.statement: The age of criminal responsibility is the same worldwide.
187.correction: The age of criminal responsibility varies across countries. For example, in Grenada and Trinidad and Tobago it’s seven, while in Spain it’s 14.

5421.belief: Only people in power can take effective action.
5421.statement: Only people in power can take effective action.
5421.correction: Every citizen can take effective action to make lasting change to their local, national or global community. You do not need to be in a position of power to take effective action.

5793.correction: Pressure groups can lobby MPs and protest for change but usually in a peaceful way. There is a wide range of different pressure groups in the UK using peaceful methods to perform effective action and bring lasting change.

4234.correction: You can lobby MPs, local councillors and any politicans to try and influence change. Any decision-maker can be lobbied.

924.belief: Very few changemakers make lasting change.
924.statement: Very few changemakers make lasting change.
924.correction: There are many examples, both throughout history and modern-day society, where changemakers have made a positive impact and lasting change.

5686.belief: Only politicians and people in important jobs can contribute to a select committee.
5686.statement: Only politicians and people in important jobs can contribute to a select committee.
5686.correction: Anyone can submit evidence to a select committee, including pupils.

2596.belief: Effective change only happens through large, dramatic actions or protests and smaller efforts don't make a difference.
2596.statement: Effective change only happens through large, dramatic actions or protests and smaller efforts don't make a difference.
2596.correction: Effective change can happen in many ways. While protests like those led by the women's suffrage movement can bring attention to important issues, smaller actions, like community policing, can also lead to significant and lasting change.

4564.belief: All men had the right to vote before 1918.
4564.statement: All men had the right to vote before 1918.
4564.correction: Approximately 40% of men could not vote before 1918.

958.belief: The Chartists achieved their aims and Parliament adopted their charter.
958.statement: The Chartists achieved their aims and Parliament adopted their charter.
958.correction: The charter was not adopted by Parliament and the next Reform Act wasn't passed until 1867, after the Chartists had disbanded.

11047.belief: As women now have the same voting rights as men in the UK, they are equally represented in the Government and Parliament.
11047.statement: As women now have the same voting rights as men in the UK, they are equally represented in the Government and Parliament.
11047.correction: This is not the case in the UK. However, as of the 2024 General Election, 40.5% of MPs in the House of Commons are female, which is the highest number ever recorded of female MPs.

5402.belief: All people who are eligible will vote in general elections.
5402.statement: All people who are eligible will vote in general elections.
5402.correction: Just because someone is eligible, it doesn't mean they will vote. In the UK 2024 general election, voter turnout was 59.7%. This was the lowest turnout at a general election since 2001.

2140.belief: Currently no 16- and 17-year-olds have the right to vote in elections in the UK.
2140.statement: Currently no 16- and 17-year-olds have the right to vote in elections in the UK.
2140.correction: In Scotland and Wales, you can vote from the age of 16 in Senedd, Scottish Parliament, and local elections.

10897.belief: Voting is the only way you can exercise your democratic rights.
10897.statement: Voting is the only way you can exercise your democratic rights.
10897.correction: There are several ways you can exercise your democratic rights, even if you cannot vote. You could: contact your local councillor or Member of Parliament (MP); express your opinion; join a peaceful protest or pressure group or join a political party.

228.belief: There are no alternatives to plastic.
228.statement: There are no alternatives to plastic.
228.correction: There are lots of alternatives to plastic that are easier to break down or recycle and therefore have less of an environmental impact, for example, glass and metal.

1714.belief: Climate change is just a natural part of Earth’s cycles, and humans aren't responsible for it.
1714.statement: Climate change is just a natural part of Earth’s cycles, and humans aren't responsible for it.
1714.correction: While Earth’s climate has naturally changed in the past, the IPCC shows that the current rapid warming is mainly caused by human activities, like burning fossil fuels and deforestation.

3141.belief: Fracking shale gas is more environmentally friendly than other gas and fossil fuels.
3141.statement: Fracking shale gas is more environmentally friendly than other gas and fossil fuels.
3141.correction: Whilst shale gas releases less CO2 than coal and oil, it is still not a renewable energy source and has several other negative environmental impacts, such as using huge amounts of water.

10120.belief: You can take legal action if your human rights are abused by anyone.
10120.statement: You can take legal action if your human rights are abused by anyone.
10120.correction: You cannot take legal action for violations by private individuals, like a friend. You can only take action against a public authority if they’ve breached your human rights.

10230.belief: There’s no way an individual or national organisation can make a difference to tackling global poverty.
10230.statement: There’s no way an individual or national organisation can make a difference to tackling global poverty.
10230.correction: There are many NGOs, global organisations and communities that are working hard to make a difference to global poverty.

3749.belief: As an individual, I am not responsible for taking action on global issues.
3749.statement: As an individual, I am not responsible for taking action on global issues.
3749.correction: You can make a difference by being an active citizen and taking responsible action.

5808.belief: The Prime Minister and the Cabinet have total control over the UK.
5808.statement: The Prime Minister and the Cabinet have total control over the UK.
5808.correction: The Prime Minister leads the Government but must answer to Parliament. Members of Parliament (MPs) debate and approve laws and can challenge a Prime Minister. The Cabinet makes decisions but is accountable to Parliament and the law.

1690.belief: The Civil Service is a political body.
1690.statement: The Civil Service is a political body.
1690.correction: The Civil Service is designed to be impartial, serving the Government of the day. Civil servants are expected to provide objective advice and implement policy without political bias. This allows for continuity even when political leadership changes.

2330.belief: Devolved governments can make laws and policies on any issue in their devolved region.
2330.statement: Devolved governments can make laws and policies on any issue in their devolved region.
2330.correction: The powers of devolved governments are limited to specific policy areas defined by devolution agreements. Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales have some executive and legislative powers. English regional governments only have some executive powers.

2233.belief: Democracy exists in all countries, just in different ways.
2233.statement: Democracy exists in all countries, just in different ways.
2233.correction: Democracy exists in many countries and the levels of it vary. However, in many countries, there is a large mix of democratic and non-democratic practices, and in others, there is no true democracy at all, with the government taking full control.

582.belief: Because both countries are democracies, the UK and the US political systems are the same.
582.statement: Because both countries are democracies, the UK and the US political systems are the same.
582.correction: Both countries are democracies but they differ: for example, the UK has a parliamentary system where only the House of Commons is elected, while the US has a presidential system where voters elect both houses of Congress and the President separately.

8895.belief: Representative democracies take away the choices of citizens because the representatives make all the decisions on their behalf.
8895.statement: Representative democracies take away the choices of citizens because the representatives make all the decisions on their behalf.
8895.correction: In a representative democracy, citizens elect representatives to make decisions on their behalf, but they can also influence policies through voting in elections, contacting their representatives and sometimes even through referendums.

2715.belief: Equality means treating everyone the same, so that’s the fairest thing to do.
2715.statement: Equality means treating everyone the same, so that’s the fairest thing to do.
2715.correction: Treating everyone the same is not always fair. Equality gives the same to all, but equity gives people what they need to have the same chance and opportunities. Equality is about meeting different needs, not pretending everyone is the same.

5722.belief: Positive stereotypes don’t cause any harm because they seem complimentary.
5722.statement: Positive stereotypes don’t cause any harm because they seem complimentary.
5722.correction: Positive stereotypes can be damaging because they create pressure for individuals to meet unrealistic expectations, ignore individuality, and reinforce limiting roles and ideas about what people should be like.

2410.belief: Discrimination only affects someone in the moment it happens.
2410.statement: Discrimination only affects someone in the moment it happens.
2410.correction: The effects can be long-lasting and deeply personal. Discrimination can lead to emotional distress, loss of confidence and reduced life opportunities. Even if an incident seems small to others, it can be big to the person being discriminated against.

10334.belief: Times have changed: everyone is already treated equally, so we do not really need equality laws anymore.
10334.statement: Times have changed: everyone is already treated equally, so we do not really need equality laws anymore.
10334.correction: While progress has been made, unfair treatment still happens. Equality laws are there to protect people and make sure everyone gets a fair chance, especially those who might otherwise be left out or discriminated against.
